heishui-river-resort.title: Heishui River Resort
texts:
4
Heishui River Resort
Heishui River Resort is a hospitality project that merges nature, architecture, and human experience. Inspired by the Blackwater River, the design creates seasonal, water-adjacent spaces that integrate local culture,
wellness, and immersive tourism. With around 100 hotel rooms and 50 boutique homestays, the architecture blends dark tones, mountain-inspired forms, and native vegetation to harmonize with the river landscape.
As part of the design team, I was involved in the early concept stage, contributing to site planning, room layout strategies, and the development of spatial concepts that guided the overall
masterplan. Our focus was on creating a resort that retreats into its environment while enhancing guest experience through circulation, micro-ecosystems, and a symbiotic relationship with
the surrounding ecology. The project has since won the competition and is currently under construction in China, positioning itself as both a cultural destination and an ecological landscape.

During the early design stage of the Heishui River Resort, I was responsible for developing the overall spatial
planning and refining the layout of different room typologies and public buildings. Working closely with the
design director, I proposed the initial massing strategy that responded to the site’s natural topography and river
orientation, ensuring a seamless transition between private villas, shared courtyards, and communal facilities. My
role involved translating conceptual massing into detailed spatial plans—optimising circulation, view corridors, and
spatial hierarchy to balance privacy and openness across the resort. The resulting layout established a coherent
relationship between architecture and landscape, forming the foundation for the project’s later development and
successful competition outcome.

12/2025- 01/2026 / SITE: Paris, France
A couture headpiece created for Germanier Paris Haute Couture SS26, developed as a wearable micro-structure inspired by the
flower’s lifecycle—growth, collapse, and decay. At Ivy J Studio, I was responsible for translating the initial artistic direction into a
structurally stable, lightweight construction, resolving how the piece could hold its form on the body without failure.
As the assistant designer, I supported design decisions through fast 3D iteration and parametric exploration, developing lace-like
digtial textures and controlled deformations that simulate organic rupture. Through repeated 3D printing tests and prototyping, we
refined the internal framework and surface geometry, aligning digital complexity with real material behaviour to deliver a runway-
ready piece where ornament emerges from structure.

tide-rewoven.title: Tide-ReWoven
texts:
12
Tide Rewoven reimagines Aberdeen’s waterfront in Hong Kong as a floating, adaptive market that responds to tides, light, and ecological pressures. Rising seas, tidal surges, and declining marine biodiversity
challenge both community and economy, while conventional infrastructure remains static. Inspired by Micrasterias and algae’s phototropic efficiency, roof structures and membranes made from fishnet-chitosan
composites shift in porosity and density according to environmental conditions. Through tidal platforms, crystallizing membranes, and weather-shaped structures, it proposes a circular spatial system—one that
grows with environmental rhythms and daily use, becoming a living interface between ecology, economy, and time. Machine learning simulations anticipate environmental variations, embedding adaptability
into both form and performance.
Bird-eye perspective render.
T i d e - R e W o v e n
BIO-INTEGRATED DESIGN YR 2 MASTER / GROUP RESEARCH PROJECT 10/2024 - 06/2025 / SITE: Aberdeen Harbour , Hong Kong, China
Research process video.

13
Early research into Aberdeen’s waterfront revealed both ecological and spatial challenges. The constructed breakwater slows tidal exchange, leading to stagnation, pollution, and declining marine biodiversity, while persistent southeast winds and strong solar exposure add further
stress. Spatial analysis identified three major zones: the fish market, the boat repair yard, and the waterfront parking area. Among these, the market emerged as the main focus due to its congested layout and obstructed connection between sea and city. Fishermen must navigate
around parked vehicles to unload catches, while customers are funnelled through narrow, unsafe passages. Building on these observations, the project advances with a re-imagined fish market that integrates site waste into adaptive structures, creating a dynamic layout responsive
to tidal conditions and the changing needs of both ecology and community.

DYNAMIC DESIGN // CIRCULAR LIFE CYCLE
The market is designed as a living system that changes with the tides,
where rising and falling water levels are reshaping spaces functions
throughout the day. Where section maps how tidal rhythms, boat arrivals,
and market routines generate shifting zones for unloading, trading, and
gathering. Floating bridges are adaptive, adjusting to boat routes and
pedestrian pathways as they gather or move apart in response to activity.
Materials are developed within a circular system, where chitosan and
shell-based composites are able to decompose, reform, and reintegrate,
allowing construction to follow the same cycles as its environment. In
this way, the market is not fixed but continuously reorganized by both
ecological forces and human presence.

This study examined how Micrasterias algae adapt their morphology to environmental changes, translating this responsiveness into generative
design logic. Controlled variations of light and nutrients revealed light intensity as the key factor shaping complexity. Time-lapse microscopy
produced datasets used to train a GAN model, enabling biological adaptation to inform dynamic material and spatial transformations in design.

17
The roof system achieves dynamic spatial complexity through the aggregation of
individual tiles responding to varying light conditions based on the machine learning
results. Each tile adjusts its curvature in real time: flattening under intense sunlight
to minimize thermal absorption, curling maximally under moderate light to increase
shading depth, and settling into a mid-state under low light to balance brightness and
shadow. These micro-adjustments scale across the entire surface, generating a living
roof scape whose form continuously shifts with the sun. As the environmental conditions
change, the complexity of the roof’s geometry intensifies or relaxes accordingly, ensuring
energy-efficient performance through a system of distributed, light-responsive modules.

MycoTerra redefines architecture by shifting its role from static shelter to an active participant in ecological cycles. Integrating mycelium fabrication with earth construction, the project embraces
circular processes of growth, decay, and renewal, moving beyond conventional linear building methods. By working with living materials, the design respects their transformation over time and explores
transitions between life and death, solid and void. Through material science, geometric design, and digital fabrication, MycoTerra responds to site-specific environmental conditions, creating micro-
environments that nurture both human occupation and fungal growth. At its core, the project highlights a symbiotic relationship between biological and built systems—where human use and mycelial
development influence one another, generating spaces that evolve, adapt, and regenerate. By embracing the biological processes and life cycles of the soil–mycelium composite, this living system
dynamically renders itself over time, in contrast to the static urban context. (Designed with Yingying Yan & Yining Loh)

4D PRINTING ASSEMBLY
We envision the assembly of our design to be done in layers, where each layer of modules
will be cured before the next layer can be stacked and biowelded. This creates a visible
gradient as the design materialises over time. As the material continues to grow, it will
be subject to decay as well. Through mycelium growth, soil is bioremediated. Decayed
modules can be composted and reused again to print new modules, allowing the design
to evolve over time. By involving human, biological, and environmental agents in the
design process, our project hopes to give the public food for thought, to rethink of the
built environment as an ecosystem that we inhabit

CO-Silo Ferry Station is located in Wynard Point, Auckland, New Zealand, surrounded by pacific coral reefs and oceanic sea creatures. The site was a reclaimed land where used to storage fuels. The design
inspiration of the ferry station was to create a bridge between human and nature. Allowing the passengers to understand the dangerous stages that sea creatures are facing now, see the parts that were hidden
under the water. By focusing on the decaying of coral reefs, the overall design was carried out through the question: “ To what extend could architecture become a living creature that evolve and became part of
the ecology.” The site has six existing silos that were used as fuel storage. In this project I want to reverse its purpose. Rather than creating CO2, the silos are used as medians to capture CO2 and re-purpose
it to usable resource.

investigates coral growth behaviour as a generative model for form development. Through a series of simulations, the design evolves from coral-inspired spatial divisions to the creation of tubular
building envelopes and shell-like structural systems that foster both functionality and symbolic resonance. The ferry station, positioned above the ocean surface, acts as a visible manifestation

materiality, and spatial experience.

project-ecoflow.title: Project-EcoFlow
texts:
32
Project EcoFlow is a water-retaining façade system designed to mitigate the urban heat island effect, particularly in dense metropolitan areas like London’s Oxford Street. With limited green space and high carbon
emissions, these environments suffer from overheating and reduced biodiversity. The project enhances existing buildings by increasing surface area and introducing vertical moss systems, which contribute to urban
cooling and foster cohabitation with diverse species. Over time, interconnected façades aim to form a continuous vertical urban garden, inviting ecological diversity back into the city while improving environmental
performance. EcoFlow also explores architecture as a metabolic system, re-imagining buildings as living organisms. By embedding adaptive processes into the built environment, the project positions humans not
just as observers, but as active participants within an interspecies network. This creates a resilient, symbiotic model where architecture, ecology, and human activity operate as a unified system.

Project Ultra-Plant is set in a post-WW3 world, where nuclear destruction has left few liveable areas. Survivors, reliant on technology, are forced to rethink their relationship with nature, realizing a symbiotic
rather than controlling role. Project Ultra-Plant proposes a modular living system treating buildings as living organisms: humans and plants collaborate to create expandable habitats that gradually restore the
environment. The system develops in four stages, reflecting environmental clarity. As living pods increase, plant genes are collected, ultimately generating a new ecosystem. Located in Auckland’s CBD for
relative safety, the design features a central concrete core for nuclear resistance, surrounded by pods connected via plant-like veins that transfer energy and resources. Expansion of these networks supports
both human habitation and environmental recovery.

FUNDING SYSTEM
Project Ultra-Plant envisions a symbiotic living system connecting residents
to the metaverse through biological and digital exchange. Each user is
assigned a sleeping pod linked to plant-like veins that circulate nutrients
and process waste. Within the metaverse, residents design their living pods
using collected plant genes and materials, all tracked through a blockchain
network. Robots assist in gathering real-world data and resources, which are
processed by AI in the core building’s plant lab. Tested and regenerated
plant genes are then cultivated atop printed living pods, completing a closed-
loop system where human activity sustains and grows the architecture itself.

The building core functions as the central system,
collecting resources from AI vehicles, rainwater, and
solar energy through the living pods. These resources
flow via plant-like veins to the core, where the AI
classifies and redistributes them. Energy is delivered
back to residents, while human waste is absorbed by
the mycelium network as nourishment. Each living pod
is 3D-printed using materials gathered by its resident;
the core’s lower level processes these resources and
plant genes to print new pod layers. Over time, the pods
organically expand, allowing residents to emerge from
their initial sleeping space.
